## My Reasoning

I have been farming in Quzhou for over 40 years. My land is on the North China Plain — flat, fertile, and well-suited to wheat and maize. There is really only one sensible system here: **winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same ground**, two harvests per year. I have watched younger farmers chase cotton or vegetables, but at 68 with my two sons working in Shijiazhuang, I need a system I can run mostly with machines and a few hired hands at harvest. Wheat-maize lets me do that.

I manage about 10 mu. I lease an additional 5 mu from a neighbor who left for the city, so 15 mu total — all going into the rotation.

For wheat, I will plant Jimai 22, an improved variety I have used for years. It lodges less than the old cultivars and performs well on our medium-fertility soil. I will apply nitrogen at a split rate — two-thirds as base fertilizer before tillage, one-third at jointing. I have seen the extension reports from China Agricultural University's station here in Quzhou. The soil is already phosphorus-rich from decades of over-application. I will cut back on phosphorus compared to what I did ten years ago. I will irrigate three times: the "winter water" (冬水) in November to protect against freeze, again at jointing in April, and at heading in May. I will skip the grain-fill irrigation — our well is getting deeper every year and I want to be careful.

For maize, I seed directly into the wheat stubble the same week I harvest wheat — no-tillage, straight in. Hybrid seed, standard commercial variety available at the county supply station. Summer rainfall in July and August usually covers most of what maize needs. I will only irrigate once, at the big bell stage (大喇叭口期), if it looks dry. I apply a single herbicide pass right after emergence. That is all the pesticide maize needs most years here.

I do not grow vegetables or fruit trees. My back cannot handle that work anymore, and the market prices are too unpredictable for me to manage the risk at my age.
